title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
gist: AWS doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes (the first change since 2018), citing agentic AI, transcoding and batch workloads; practitioners warn of doubled concurrency needs, SQS/stream/NAT side constraints and cost, and some read the move as a competitive response to Google Cloud Run's 60-minute limit.

insights.claim: AWS doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes for synchronous, asynchronous and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and with no opt-in; the 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018 (after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015).
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Expands the addressable workload set for serverless compute, potentially shifting spend from containers to Lambda.
insights.locator: AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout

insights.claim: AWS Lambda now has three shapes with different limits: Web Functions keep 15 minutes, Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, and on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations get 30 minutes while asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September 2026.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is fragmenting Lambda into product tiers to capture long-running workloads, raising product-choice complexity.
insights.locator: The change covers one of the three shapes

insights.claim: AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations and report generation as the workloads that outgrew Lambda's 15-minute limit.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Agentic AI is directly reshaping cloud primitive design — a demand signal for long-running serverless compute.

insights.claim: AWS's announcement authors note that Lambda concurrency equals requests per second times average duration, so a 30-minute function needs twice the concurrency of a 15-minute one — 1 request per second at 30 minutes needs 1,800 concurrent executions.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Longer timeouts increase concurrency quota and cost exposure; capacity planning is the first check.
insights.quote: Concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds.
insights.locator: the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity

insights.claim: Surrounding services constrain 30-minute Lambdas: an SQS visibility timeout should be at least six times the function timeout (three hours), Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams process one batch per shard so slow functions slow the shard, Amazon MQ/DocumentDB/Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes, a NAT gateway drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and Init keeps its 10-second limit.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The headline limit overstates practical gains; architecture around the function determines usability.
insights.locator: The rest of the post is about what sits around the function

insights.claim: Independent AWS practitioner Wibo van der Sluis found in eu-west-1 testing that Lambda only checks the SQS visibility-timeout rule at mapping creation, and then compares the queue against the function timeout itself rather than six times it, so the six-times rule must be self-enforced.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Misconfigurations can slip past AWS validation, a reliability risk for teams adopting long timeouts.
insights.quote: So the check exists, but only at creation.
insights.locator: Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner

insights.claim: An asynchronous Lambda function that times out three times at the new limit runs for 90 minutes before its event reaches a dead-letter queue, which van der Sluis argues makes 30 minutes the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Longer timeouts can mask failures and delay error handling.
insights.locator: He adds that an asynchronous function

themes.theme: Practitioner skepticism on cost and fit

insights.claim: Former AWS employee Magnus Eriksson notes Lambda is quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2 and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Price-per-compute limits how much long-running batch work actually migrates to Lambda.
insights.quote: is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2
insights.locator: The comments under the post took two directions

insights.claim: AWS DevTools Hero Matthew Bonig predicts the Lambda timeout will eventually reach 8 hours, blurring the line with Lambda MicroVMs so that nobody will understand when to use which.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Product overlap within AWS serverless may confuse buyers.
insights.quote: Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs.

insights.claim: Reddit commenters welcomed the 30-minute Lambda limit as a way to avoid Fargate and ECS for long batch jobs, while others cautioned that long runs bill the full duration at configured memory and that Step Functions with Fargate or ECS remains cleaner for multi-step or stateful work.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Some cannibalisation of Fargate/ECS batch usage is plausible, but containers remain preferred for complex jobs.
insights.quote: A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory

insights.claim: AWS Serverless Hero Luc van Donkersgoed reacted ambivalently to 30-minute Lambda timeouts, calling it a moment where hell froze over.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Even serverless advocates see the change as a philosophical shift for Lambda.
insights.quote: Hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.
insights.locator: Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS

themes.theme: Competitive pressure from Cloud Run and Azure

insights.claim: Branch Insurance CTO Joseph Emison reads the Lambda timeout increase as the Lambda team recognizing that Google Cloud Run, which allows 60 minutes per request, is its most compelling competitor; Azure Functions on Flex Consumption and Premium plans enforce no maximum timeout.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Serverless limits are a competitive axis among AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure; watch for further AWS moves.
insights.locator: Joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance

insights.claim: AWS has not said whether the Lambda timeout limit will move again beyond 30 minutes.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Further increases remain an open question to monitor.
insights.locator: AWS has not said whether the Lambda limit will move again
